Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette: Sarah, a 19-year-old North American woman, has been struggling to find her footing since she was assaulted nearly six months ago. Now married and unemployed, Sarah's life is deeply impacted by the traumatic event that continues to haunt her. The assault occurred during a late night out with friends at a local bar. The smell of alcohol still lingers in Sarah’s memory, evoking intense distress whenever she encounters it. That night, an altercation broke out near their table when a group of men began shouting aggressively in Arabic. Before anyone could react, one man approached her from behind and dragged her into a secluded area outside the bar, where he assaulted her. Since that terrifying night, Sarah has developed a heightened sensitivity to specific triggers. The sound of motorcycles is particularly distressing, reminding her of the roar of the engine as she escaped from her assailant. Similarly, any shouting in Arabic immediately transports her back to the frightening event. She had come to believe that these sounds were harbingers of danger and could signal another assault. Sarah has adopted several maladaptive strategies to cope with her fears. She avoids anniversaries connected to the event, making every effort to disengage from any activities or memories associated with that night. Going out at night has become intolerable for Sarah; she is certain that being outside after dark increases her vulnerability. Additionally, Sarah tries not to pay attention to or look at her own body, as it serves as a constant reminder of the assault. Sarah’s hyper-vigilance is evident in her everyday life. She frequently listens for any sounds that might indicate someone entering her home, and she checks behind her multiple times to ensure no one is following her. These behaviors have become so ingrained that they dominate her daily routine. Flashbacks are a frequent occurrence; sometimes, she suddenly feels as if the assault were happening again, causing her to lose touch with reality. The memories of the traumatic event intrude upon Sarah’s life without warning. The auditory and olfactory details from that night replay in her mind with startling clarity. When Sarah thinks about what happened, she can hear the shouting in Arabic and smell the alcohol, which triggers a powerful sense of fear and distress. Sarah's beliefs about the world have been shattered by this experience. She feels that everything she once held true has been completely destroyed, leaving her with a profound sense of disillusionment. Her ability to do what defined her before the assault has diminished; she no longer engages in activities she once enjoyed. Moreover, Sarah often thinks that someone else would have stopped the event from happening, adding a layer of self-blame and regret. Sarah’s husband has noticed the changes in her behavior but struggles to understand why she withdraws so frequently or becomes overwhelmed by seemingly minor triggers. Their relationship has been strained as a result, with both feeling frustrated by their inability to bridge this gap. What finally brought Sarah to seek help was an intense episode of flashbacks and distress during what would have been the anniversary of her assault. She realized that avoiding these anniversaries was no longer sustainable and that she needed professional support to manage her symptoms effectively. Her primary fear is reliving the trauma, but she also hopes for a sense of normalcy and peace in her life once again. Sarah’s current state is marked by an overwhelming need for safety and control. She seeks help with the hope that through therapy, she can regain some semblance of a life free from constant fear and distress.
